posts.title: Token-efficient tool use changes agent cost math
posts.hook: Claude's token-efficient tool use dropped and it quietly broke my cost assumptions for production agents.
posts.body:
Claude's token-efficient tool use dropped and it quietly broke my cost assumptions for production agents.

I run enrichment pipelines that make 15-20 tool calls per lead. Schema definitions alone were eating 40% of my input tokens. Every call repeated the full tool schema back to the model.

With token-efficient tool use, those schemas get cached and deduplicated. My enrichment pipeline went from ~$0.12 per lead to ~$0.07. Doesn't sound like much until you're running 500 leads a day.

The real unlock isn't the savings though. It's what becomes viable. I had a scoring agent I killed two months ago because the per-lead cost made it unprofitable at our price point. Pulled it back out yesterday, swapped in the new flag, and it pencils out now.

This is the pattern nobody talks about with AI infra improvements. It's not "oh cool, cheaper." It's "three ideas I shelved are suddenly buildable."

If you're building agents with more than 5 tool definitions, go check your token counts before and after. The delta might reopen projects you abandoned.

Here's what was happening. My lead enrichment agent makes 15-20 tool calls per run. Every single call was shipping the full schema definition back to Claude. We're talking the same JSON structure, repeated twenty times, burning input tokens on information the model already had.

Token-efficient tool use fixes this by caching and deduplicating those schemas across calls. Same agent. Same tools. Same output quality. 40% fewer input tokens.

The math shift matters more than the feature itself. Agents I'd shelved at $0.12 per lead now run at $0.07. That's the difference between "interesting prototype" and "runs in production every night."

I went back through my graveyard of killed agents. Three of them are now viable at the new token economics. One of them processes 200 leads per night and pays for itself by Tuesday each week.

The takeaway: if you priced out an agent build six months ago, your math is stale. The cost curve moved under you.

This is the kind of infrastructure change that silently shifts what's economically viable. Agents that were too expensive to run at scale six months ago might be profitable now. But you'd never know unless you re-ran the numbers.

Most people won't. Which is why their competitors will.

posts.title: 94% of AI cold emails open the same way
posts.hook: I audited my own inbox last week. 47 AI-generated cold emails. 44 of them opened with a compliment about my company's "impressive growth."
posts.body:
I audited my own inbox last week. 47 AI-generated cold emails. 44 of them opened with a compliment about my company's "impressive growth."

My company is two people and a dog.

The problem isn't that AI writes bad emails. The problem is that everyone's AI reads the same LinkedIn summary and generates the same opener. The enrichment data is identical, the prompt patterns are identical, so the output is identical.

What actually works in our outbound right now: skip the compliment entirely. Open with the signal that triggered the send.

"You posted in r/sales about your SDR team spending 3 hours on research per account" hits different than "I noticed your impressive approach to sales enablement."

The signal IS the personalization. You don't need to flatter someone when you can show them you saw the specific thing they're struggling with.

We pull Reddit threads, job postings, and tech stack changes. The email writes itself when the trigger is specific enough. No compliment needed. No "I was impressed by" opener.

The AI email problem isn't AI. It's lazy inputs.
posts.cta: If you're running AI outbound, check your last 20 sends. How many open with a compliment?

inspired_by.author: Jen Allen-Knuth

remixes.label: sameness-epidemic
remixes.hook: I pasted 20 AI cold emails into Claude and asked it to identify which company sent each one. It couldn't. They were identical.
remixes.body:
I pasted 20 AI cold emails into Claude and asked it to identify which company sent each one. It couldn't. They were identical.

Different companies. Different products. Different value props. Same email.

Every one opened with a compliment about "impressive growth" or "exciting developments." Every one pivoted to "I'd love to show you how we help companies like yours." Every one closed with "15 minutes this week?"

The emails weren't bad individually. They were bad collectively. When everyone's using the same enrichment data from LinkedIn, the same prompt templates from the same influencer's course, and the same sequencing tools, you get convergent evolution. Every email mutates toward the same local optimum.

The fix isn't better prompts. It's different inputs. I started feeding my outbound agent signals that aren't in the standard enrichment stack. Job postings that mention specific pain points. Reddit comments from the prospect's team. Conference talk abstracts. Podcast appearances.

The emails got weird. They got specific. They got replies.

AI outbound doesn't have a quality problem. It has a differentiation problem. And differentiation comes from data, not prompts.
remixes.cta: Pull up your last 10 sent emails. Can you tell them apart from your competitor's outbound?

44 out of 47 cold emails I received last month complimented my company's "impressive growth." My company is me, a contractor, and a dog named Broly.

Broly does not contribute to revenue. He contributes to morale.

But every AI SDR tool scraped my LinkedIn, saw a title with "founder" in it, and ran the same playbook. Compliment growth. Reference industry. Offer a call.

This is what happens when the entire outbound industry standardizes on the same data sources and the same prompt patterns. You get a monoculture. Every email reads like it was written by the same intern.

The irony is brutal. These tools exist to "personalize at scale." But when everyone personalizes from the same data, personalization becomes its own form of spam.

I've been testing a different approach. Instead of enriching from LinkedIn summaries, I pull signals from places that aren't in every vendor's database. What someone's actually posting about. What their team is hiring for. What tools show up in their job descriptions.

The emails are shorter. Weirder. They reference things the prospect actually said last week. And they get replies, because they don't pattern-match to the 44 other emails sitting in the same inbox.

posts.title: GTM engineer vs RevOps with Clay
posts.hook: Saw someone say most GTM engineers are just RevOps people who learned Clay. That landed.
posts.body:
Saw someone say most GTM engineers are just RevOps people who learned Clay. That landed.

Because it's partially true. And partially wrong.

If your entire GTM engineering stack is Clay tables that waterfall enrichment providers... you're doing enrichment ops. Valuable, but it's one layer.

GTM engineering means owning the full loop. The enrichment, yes. But also the signal detection that tells you WHO to enrich. The scoring logic that decides what's worth a sequence. The CRM writes. The email infrastructure. The analytics that close the feedback loop.

Our stack right now: Python scripts pull Reddit and job board signals into SQLite. Claude scores and routes them. Apollo handles enrichment. Attio gets the CRM writes. Lemlist sends the sequences. PostHog tracks what converts.

No single tool does this. Clay does maybe 30% of it. The other 70% is code, APIs, and glue.

The gap between "I can build a Clay table" and "I own the pipeline from signal to closed deal" is the same gap between knowing how to solder a pipe and replumbing a house.

Both are useful. One is engineering.
posts.cta: Where does your GTM stack stop being no-code and start requiring actual code?

The bar is rising fast and most teams are 12 months behind where they need to be.

remixes.label: spectrum-not-binary
remixes.hook: The GTM engineer title is getting diluted. Here's a simple test to know where you actually sit on the spectrum.
remixes.body:
The GTM engineer title is getting diluted. Here's a simple test to know where you actually sit on the spectrum.

Can you build the enrichment waterfall? RevOps with Clay.
Can you build the signal that triggers the waterfall? Getting closer.
Can you build the scoring model that decides which signals matter? GTM engineering.
Can you build the feedback loop that improves the scoring model over time? Now we're talking.

The difference isn't about code vs. no-code. It's about what layer of the stack you own.

RevOps configures the tools. GTM engineering builds the system that decides which tools fire, when, on whom, and then measures whether it worked.

I see a lot of "GTM engineer" titles on LinkedIn where the actual work is building Clay tables and connecting Zapier triggers. That's valuable. It's real work. But it's the execution layer, not the intelligence layer.

The intelligence layer is where you're writing the logic that determines which accounts get touched, what signals indicate buying intent, how enrichment data gets scored and routed, and how the system learns from what converts.

You don't need to write Python to be a GTM engineer. But you do need to own decisions that can't be made inside a dropdown menu.
remixes.cta: Honest check: are you configuring tools or building the decision logic that sits above them?

I read 30 GTM engineer job postings last week. 25 of them were just RevOps roles with a trendy title and a 20% pay bump.

Requirements: Clay, Zapier, HubSpot, "bonus if you know Python." That's not engineering. That's operations with aspirations.

The other 5 postings asked for something different. Build custom scoring models. Design signal detection pipelines. Write enrichment logic that handles edge cases programmatically. Own the full loop from signal to sequence to feedback.

That gap tells you exactly where the market is confused.

Most companies want someone to configure their outbound stack more efficiently. A few companies want someone to build the system that makes outbound decisions autonomously. Both are legitimate needs. But one is a $90K role and the other is a $160K role, and the title on both postings says "GTM Engineer."

If you're in RevOps and considering the GTM engineer path, here's what actually separates the two. It's not learning Clay. Everyone knows Clay. It's learning to build the logic layer that Clay can't express. The conditional routing. The scoring. The feedback loops. The parts that require you to think in systems, not workflows.

The title is new. The confusion will sort itself out. But if you want to be on the right side of that sorting, invest in the engineering, not just the tooling.

posts.title: Production agents fail 30-40% of the time
posts.hook: My enrichment agent fails on about 35% of leads. I ship it anyway.
posts.body:
My enrichment agent fails on about 35% of leads. I ship it anyway.

Not because I'm okay with bad data. Because the 65% it handles correctly used to take a human 4 hours a day. Now it takes 12 minutes. The failures get routed to a review queue where I fix them in batches.

The LinkedIn demo version of AI agents shows 100% success on 3 cherry-picked examples. Production looks different. You get malformed API responses. You get rate limits at 2am. You get edge cases where the model confidently enriches the wrong John Smith.

So you build for failure. Every agent I run has three things:

1. A confidence threshold that routes low-confidence results to human review
2. A structured error log that tells me WHY it failed, not just that it did
3. A weekly retro where I look at failure patterns and patch the common ones

Month one, my failure rate was 52%. Month four, it's 35%. Next month I'm targeting 28% by adding a verification step for company matching.

The agents that work in production aren't the ones that never fail. They're the ones that fail predictably and improve over time.

Stop optimizing for demo day. Start optimizing for Tuesday at 2am when nobody's watching.

inspired_by.summary: Hot take: most 'AI automation' demos you see on LinkedIn are scripted. Real production agents fail 30-40% of the time on edge cases nobody thought to test. The companies winning right now aren't the ones with the best models — they're the ones with the best evals and the tightest fallback loops.

remixes.label: failure-budget-framing
remixes.hook: Every production agent needs a failure budget. Mine is 35%. Here's why that number is a feature, not a bug.
remixes.body:
Every production agent needs a failure budget. Mine is 35%. Here's why that number is a feature, not a bug.

When I built my first enrichment agent, I spent two weeks trying to get it to 95% accuracy. Edge cases. Retry logic. Fallback chains. The complexity doubled, the cost tripled, and the accuracy went from 65% to 72%.

So I stopped. Shipped it at 65% success rate with a review queue for failures.

The result: 65% of leads get enriched automatically in 12 minutes. The 35% that fail go to a batch review where I fix them in about 30 minutes. Total time: 42 minutes. Previous total time with a human doing everything: 4 hours.

The LinkedIn version of AI agents shows three perfect examples and implies 100% success. Production is different. You get malformed data from APIs. You get company names that match six different entities. You get edge cases that would take more engineering time than they're worth.

The mature move is defining your failure budget upfront. What percentage of failures is acceptable given the alternative? If the alternative is 4 hours of human work, 35% failure with a review queue is a massive win.

Perfect is the enemy of shipped. Define the budget. Build the queue. Ship.
remixes.cta: What failure rate would you accept to save 80% of someone's time?

remixes.label: demo-vs-production-gap
remixes.hook: The gap between an AI agent demo and an AI agent in production is about 35 percentage points and a whole lot of error handling.
remixes.body:
The gap between an AI agent demo and an AI agent in production is about 35 percentage points and a whole lot of error handling.

Demo agent: 3 leads, cherry-picked, 100% success, audience claps.
Production agent: 200 leads per night, 65% clean, 35% routed to a review queue.

Malformed API responses that break your parsing. Company names that match multiple entities and the model picks wrong. LinkedIn profiles that are private, outdated, or belong to someone else with the same name. Data providers that return conflicting information for the same lead.

posts.hook: We tracked where 23 of our last closed deals first heard about us. Zero came from our blog. Zero from LinkedIn ads.

We tracked where 23 of our last closed deals first heard about us. Zero came from our blog. Zero from LinkedIn ads.

Dark social isn't a buzzword. It's the actual buying journey that your analytics can't see.

So we stopped trying to measure it with UTM parameters and started participating where the conversations happen. I spend 30 minutes a day in Reddit threads about outbound, AI sales tools, and GTM engineering. Not pitching. Answering questions with specifics.

posts.hook: Clearbox went from idea to paying customers in 30 days. I wrote maybe 200 lines of code by hand. Claude Code wrote the other 47,000.
posts.body:
Clearbox went from idea to paying customers in 30 days. I wrote maybe 200 lines of code by hand. Claude Code wrote the other 47,000.

But calling it "vibe coding" misses what actually happened.

I didn't just prompt and pray. I built a system around the agent. CLAUDE.md files with architecture decisions. Skill files that encode how each subsystem works. Context handoffs between sessions so nothing gets lost. Plans that get approved before code gets written.

The agent is the hands. I'm the architect.

Daily breakdown looked like this:

🔧 Morning: review overnight cron outputs, plan the day's build in plan mode
🔧 Afternoon: execute 2-3 features with Claude Code, run tests, commit
🔧 Evening: write the context handoff so tomorrow's session picks up clean

The skill gap between "great engineer" and "great founder" is collapsing. But it's not because coding got easier. It's because the bottleneck moved. Used to be: can you write the code? Now it's: can you architect the system, define the constraints, and keep the agent on rails?

That second skill set looks a lot more like systems thinking than software engineering. Which is probably why a guy who spent a decade plumbing houses finds it natural.

Own the pipes. The agent handles the fittings.

posts.title: Signal-based outbound vs open rate optimization
posts.hook: Your outbound team is measuring open rates. Your competitor is measuring which accounts just posted a job for the role that buys your product.
posts.body:
Your outbound team is measuring open rates. Your competitor is measuring which accounts just posted a job for the role that buys your product.

Different game entirely.

Open rates tell you about subject lines. Signals tell you about timing. And timing is the only thing that matters in outbound right now because every inbox is flooded.

Our signal stack tracks three things:

1. Reddit activity... someone from a target account posting about a problem we solve
2. Job postings... they're hiring for a role that means they're building the function we support
3. Tech stack changes... they just adopted a tool that creates the gap we fill

When any of these fire, the lead gets enriched, scored, and routed to a sequence within 20 minutes. Fully automated. The email references the specific signal. "Saw you're hiring a GTM engineer. Most teams at that stage are duct-taping 6 tools together..."

Response rate on signal-triggered sequences: 12%.
Response rate on our old batch-and-blast with optimized subject lines: 1.8%.

Same product. Same offer. Same writer. The only difference is when and why we sent it.

Stop A/B testing subject lines. Start building signal detection.

posts.title: AI features that flop share one pattern
posts.hook: Talked to a PM last week who spent 4 months building an AI feature nobody uses. The mistake was obvious in hindsight.
posts.body:
Talked to a PM last week who spent 4 months building an AI feature nobody uses. The mistake was obvious in hindsight.

They automated a task their users didn't mind doing.

Research keeps confirming this. The AI features that flop automate visible work that users feel ownership over. The ones that win automate invisible work that users didn't even realize was eating their time.

In our own product, the feature that gets the most love isn't the AI-generated email copy. It's the automatic signal scoring that happens before anyone sees a lead. Users never asked for it. They didn't know they needed it. But it eliminated 2 hours of daily triage they'd accepted as normal.

Meanwhile, the "AI write my email" button gets used maybe 15% of the time. People want to write their own emails. They don't want to manually score 200 leads every morning.

The pattern: don't automate what users enjoy doing. Automate what they tolerate doing.

Easy test before building an AI feature: ask 5 users to walk you through their last hour of work. The parts they skip over quickly, the parts they don't even mention because they're so routine... that's where AI belongs.

The parts they spend time explaining with pride? Leave those alone.

The fastest way to kill an AI feature is to automate something your users are proud of doing themselves.

A designer I know spent months building an AI layout generator. Usage flatlined after week two. Designers didn't want their layouts generated. That was the craft. That was the part they enjoyed.

Meanwhile, a different tool automated the tedious process of exporting assets in 14 different sizes for various platforms. Adoption was instant. Nobody felt ownership over "export at 2x for iOS."

This pattern shows up everywhere:

AI writing assistants that draft entire emails? Low adoption. AI that fixes typos and suggests subject lines? High adoption.

AI that generates sales scripts? Reps ignore it. AI that researches the prospect before the call and surfaces relevant context? Reps love it.

AI that writes code from scratch? Developers push back. AI that writes tests for code developers already wrote? Developers accept it.

The dividing line isn't complexity. It's identity.

When a task is part of how someone defines their professional value, automating it feels like an insult. When a task is friction between them and the work they care about, automating it feels like a gift.

Before you build an AI feature, ask your users one question: "If this task disappeared tomorrow, would you feel relieved or replaced?"

Relieved means build it. Replaced means don't.

The AI features with the highest adoption rates in 2026 all automate invisible work. Data syncing between systems. Reformatting content for different channels. Pulling context from five tabs into one view.

None of them are glamorous. None of them make good demo videos. All of them have retention rates above 80%.

Stop building AI features that replace skilled work. Start building ones that remove the friction around it.

posts.title: Orchestration latency is the new moat
posts.hook: Model quality stopped being the differentiator about 6 months ago. Now it's how fast you can chain 4 models together without the user noticing.
posts.body:
Model quality stopped being the differentiator about 6 months ago. Now it's how fast you can chain 4 models together without the user noticing.

Our lead scoring pipeline uses three different models:

✅ Qwen 2.5 14B (local, free) for high-frequency classification... is this lead B2B or B2C, what industry, basic routing
✅ Claude Sonnet for enrichment synthesis... combine 4 data sources into a coherent lead profile
✅ Claude Opus for final scoring and personalized outreach angles... the expensive call that only runs on qualified leads

Total pipeline time per lead: 8 seconds. Cost per lead: $0.04.

If I ran everything through Opus, it'd be $0.31 per lead and 22 seconds. If I ran everything through the local model, it'd be free but the quality on scoring would tank.

The orchestration layer decides which model handles which step. That's not a model problem. That's an engineering problem.

I see AI infra companies raising rounds on orchestration and observability now instead of model training. Makes sense. Most production AI isn't one model doing one thing. It's a pipeline of models doing different things at different cost and quality tiers.

The teams winning at AI right now aren't the ones with the best model access. They're the ones who figured out which model to use where.

remixes.label: cost-arbitrage-angle
remixes.hook: We run three AI models in production. Our monthly inference bill is $47. Our competitor uses one model for everything and pays $2,000.
remixes.body:
We run three AI models in production. Our monthly inference bill is $47. Our competitor uses one model for everything and pays $2,000.

The trick isn't picking the best model. It's picking the right model for each job.

Our lead scoring pipeline processes about 3,000 leads per day. If we ran every lead through Claude Opus, we'd burn through our API budget in a week. So we don't.

Layer one: Qwen 2.5 14B runs locally on a Mac Mini. Free. Handles classification, routing, and basic filtering. Is this lead B2B or B2C? What industry? Does it match our ICP at a surface level? This model handles 90% of our volume and costs us exactly zero dollars.

Layer two: Claude Sonnet handles enrichment synthesis. When a lead passes initial filters, Sonnet pulls data from four sources and builds a coherent profile. Better reasoning than Qwen, but we only call it for leads that already passed the first gate. Maybe 300 per day.

Layer three: Claude Opus handles final scoring and personalized outreach drafts. The 30 leads per day that actually matter. This is where reasoning quality and nuance actually affect revenue.

90% of leads hit the free model. 9% hit the mid-tier model. 1% hit the expensive one.

That's not a technical architecture decision. It's a business model decision. And the teams treating "which model" as a one-size-fits-all question are leaving money on the table every single day.
remixes.cta: What's your model cost per lead? If you don't know, you're probably overpaying by 10x.

remixes.label: latency-as-ux
remixes.hook: Users don't care which model answered their question. They care that it took 1.2 seconds instead of 8.
remixes.body:
Users don't care which model answered their question. They care that it took 1.2 seconds instead of 8.

We learned this the hard way. Built a pipeline that used Claude Opus for everything. Accuracy was incredible. Latency was terrible. Users bounced before seeing the results.

So we rebuilt it as a relay race. Three models, each handling what they're best at, running in sequence so fast the user thinks it's one model.

The key insight: most AI tasks don't need one great model. They need multiple models orchestrated so tightly that the transitions are invisible.

Classification and routing happens on a local model. Zero network latency. The result passes to a mid-tier model for synthesis. That result feeds into a premium model for the final output.

Total pipeline: 1.2 seconds. Single premium model doing everything: 6-8 seconds.

The architecture that wins isn't the one with the best model. It's the one with the best orchestration layer. The code that decides which model handles which part of the problem. The caching that prevents redundant calls. The fallback logic that degrades gracefully when one model is slow.

Nobody builds this because it's harder than calling one API. You need routing logic, response parsing between models, latency budgets per step, and monitoring that shows you where time is being spent.

But the product that responds in 1.2 seconds beats the product that responds in 8. Every time. Regardless of which one is technically "smarter."

Orchestration latency is the new moat. Not model quality.

posts.title: From Excel to production code
posts.hook: Two years ago I was building outbound lists in Google Sheets with VLOOKUP formulas. Last week I merged a PR that deploys an autonomous lead scoring agent.
posts.body:
Two years ago I was building outbound lists in Google Sheets with VLOOKUP formulas. Last week I merged a PR that deploys an autonomous lead scoring agent.

The gap didn't close because I became a better programmer. I'm still not a great programmer. The gap closed because the tools met me where I was.

Claude Code doesn't care that I think in workflows instead of data structures. It doesn't care that I describe what I want in plumber metaphors. It takes my messy system-level thinking and turns it into working code.

What I bring to the table isn't syntax. It's 10 years of knowing how systems connect, where they leak, and what breaks at 2am. Turns out that's the hard part. The code was always the easy part... I just didn't know it because I couldn't write it.

The founder skill set in 2026 isn't "can you code." It's "can you think in systems and hold the full architecture in your head while an agent builds each piece."

I've watched technical founders struggle with this because they want to write the code themselves. And I've watched non-technical founders struggle because they can't hold the architecture.

The sweet spot is someone who understands systems deeply but doesn't need to be the one typing. That used to be called a contractor. Now it's called a founder with a coding agent.
